summary:
The page first finishes the road map: the final chapters identify **new research directions** and **review the concepts** presented across the book.

**About the code.** The book is an example of **literate programming**: it is *both* a prose explanation of deep learning *and* a runnable Python program. From **chapter 2** on, each chapter contains code listings that can be run as a **Jupyter notebook** (an interactive environment for running Python and visualizing data). The authors *strongly suggest* running, modifying and playing with the examples as you read, to build your own intuition.

All code is in **Python** with the **Keras** library. Keras can run on top of **TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX**, "the most popular low-level deep learning frameworks as of 2025". You can run everything on a local machine or in the browser with **Google Colab**, a hosted Jupyter environment.

Where to get the code:

- executable snippets in the **liveBook** version (included with print/eBook purchase);
- complete code on the **Manning website** and on **GitHub** at `github.com/fchollet/deep-learning-with-python-notebooks`, with instructions for running locally;
- the **web version** at deeplearningwithpython.io, where a **Colab link at the top of each chapter** runs that chapter's code on free hosted hardware.

**liveBook discussion forum.** Purchase includes access to liveBook, Manning's online reader, where you can attach comments to the book or to specific sections/paragraphs, make notes, ask and answer technical questions, and get help from the authors and other readers. Manning provides the venue but does **not** commit the authors to any amount of participation, which is voluntary and unpaid; the forum stays accessible while the book is in print.

**How to use this page:** set up your environment now (Colab is the zero-install option, and it gives free GPU access), so you can run chapter 2's first listings as you read.

paragraphs.excerpt: This book is an example of literate programming—it is simultaneously a prose
paragraphs.what_it_says: The book is literate programming: both a prose explanation and a runnable Python program. From chapter 2 on, chapters are interspersed with code listings runnable as Jupyter notebooks. The authors strongly suggest running, modifying and playing with the examples to build intuition.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Code is not an appendix; it is part of the explanation. Each chapter is designed to be executed top to bottom, so later listings depend on variables defined in earlier ones (e.g. a model defined in one listing is trained in the next).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Intuition in deep learning comes largely from experimentation — seeing what happens when you change a hyperparameter. Running the notebooks turns the book from something you read into something you try.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Because notebook cells share state, running listings out of order can produce confusing errors (e.g. a NameError for an undefined model or variable). Beyond the book: restart and run all cells in order when in doubt.

An interactive document of code cells and text cells; you run cells one by one and see outputs (numbers, plots) inline.

paragraphs.what_it_says: All code is Python with Keras, which runs on TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX (the most popular low-level frameworks as of 2025). Code runs locally or in the browser via Google Colab. Executable snippets are in the liveBook version; the full code is on the Manning website and on GitHub (fchollet/deep-learning-with-python-notebooks) with local-setup instructions; the web version at deeplearningwithpython.io has a Colab link at the top of each chapter to run that chapter's code on free hosted hardware.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Keras is a high-level layer; the backend (TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX) does the low-level tensor computation and differentiation. The same Keras code can run on any of the three. Colab removes installation and hardware barriers, which matches the preface's accessibility goal.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: You can start immediately without a GPU or local install. Knowing that the backend is swappable also prepares you for chapter 3, which introduces each framework.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: in Keras 3 the backend is chosen before importing Keras, e.g. via the environment variable `KERAS_BACKEND` set to `"jax"`, `"tensorflow"` or `"torch"`.

concepts.name: Literate programming
concepts.definition: Writing a program as an explanation for human readers, with executable code embedded in prose; the book calls itself 'simultaneously a prose explanation of deep learning concepts and a runnable Python program'.
concepts.intuition: A textbook whose examples are live: you can run each one.
concepts.technical: Realized here as one Jupyter notebook per chapter (from chapter 2), whose cells follow the order of the listings in the text.
concepts.significance: It is how the book delivers on 'functioning code paired with explanations' (PDF p.20).
concepts.example: Opening a chapter's Colab link from deeplearningwithpython.io and running the listings while reading.
concepts.misconception: Reading the code without running it gives much less intuition than experimenting with it.

concepts.name: Keras backend
concepts.definition: The low-level deep learning framework (TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX) on which Keras code runs.
concepts.intuition: Keras is the steering wheel; the backend is the engine.
concepts.technical: Keras expresses layers, models and training loops; the backend supplies tensor operations, automatic differentiation and GPU/TPU execution.
concepts.significance: The book's code is written once in Keras and can run on any of the three backends.
concepts.example: Running the same chapter notebook with the JAX backend or the PyTorch backend.
concepts.misconception: Keras is not a separate competitor to these frameworks; it runs on top of them.

deeper.title: A minimal setup checklist
deeper.body:
Beyond the book:

1. Easiest: open deeplearningwithpython.io, go to chapter 2, click the Colab link at the top, and run the first cells.
2. In Colab, select a GPU runtime when you reach the heavier vision and generative chapters.
3. Local alternative: clone `github.com/fchollet/deep-learning-with-python-notebooks` and follow its instructions.
4. Run cells in order; if something breaks, restart the runtime and run all.

takeaways: The book is literate programming: prose plus a runnable program, with notebooks from chapter 2 on.
All code uses Python and Keras; Keras runs on TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX.
Code runs locally or for free in Google Colab; it is available via liveBook, the Manning site, GitHub and deeplearningwithpython.io.
The liveBook forum allows paragraph-level questions, but author participation is voluntary.

questions.question: On which low-level frameworks can Keras run, according to this page?
questions.explanation: The page names all three as 'the most popular low-level deep learning frameworks as of 2025'. scikit-learn is not mentioned and is not a Keras backend.

questions.question: What does it mean that the book is an example of 'literate programming'?
questions.answer: It is simultaneously a prose explanation of deep learning concepts and a runnable Python program.
questions.explanation: This is the page's own definition; from chapter 2, code listings can be run as Jupyter notebooks.

questions.question: From which chapter do the code listings begin?
questions.explanation: 'Starting with chapter 2, each chapter will be interspersed with code listings.' Chapter 1 is conceptual; chapters 3 and 7 are later.

questions.question: Name two ways to run the book's code without installing anything locally.
questions.answer: Google Colab (hosted Jupyter notebooks), for example via the Colab link at the top of each chapter in the web version at deeplearningwithpython.io; and the executable snippets in the liveBook version.
questions.explanation: Both are described on the page; Colab runs on free hosted hardware.

questions.question: Why do the authors 'strongly suggest' modifying and playing with the examples instead of only reading them?
questions.answer: To build your own intuition about the concepts: seeing how outputs change when you change code (layer sizes, training settings) turns abstract explanations into experience.
questions.explanation: The page links running/modifying the code directly to building intuitions; this matches the code-first approach described on PDF p.20.

questions.question: What does Manning commit to regarding the liveBook forum?
options: A guaranteed response from the authors within a week
Providing a venue for dialogue, without committing the authors to any amount of participation
Paying the authors to answer questions
Keeping the forum online permanently regardless of print status
questions.answer: Providing a venue for dialogue, without committing the authors to any amount of participation
questions.explanation: Author participation is voluntary and unpaid; the forum is accessible as long as the book is in print.

questions.question: Before reading chapter 2, can you open a notebook (Colab or local) and run a cell that imports Keras? If not, follow the setup links on this page now.
questions.explanation: Having a working environment ready is the prerequisite for the book's hands-on method.
